 1             I.   WITNESS IDENTIFICATION AND QUALIFICATIONS

 2   Q.   Please state your name and business address.

 3   A.   My name is Jarred J. Cooley. My business address is 790 South Buchanan Street,

 4        Amarillo, Texas 79101.

 5   Q.   On whose behalf are you testifying in this proceeding?

 6   A.   I am filing testimony on behalf of Southwestern Public Service Company, a New

 7        Mexico corporation (“SPS”). SPS is a wholly-owned electric utility subsidiary of

 8        Xcel Energy Inc. (“Xcel Energy”).

 9   Q.   By whom are you employed and in what position?

10   A.   I am employed by SPS as Director, Strategic Planning.

11   Q.   Please briefly outline your responsibilities as Director, Strategic Planning.

12   A.   I am responsible for leading and directing Xcel Energy-wide teams to plan and

13        implement strategic business projects for SPS. In that role, I work with generation

14        and transmission planning teams on long-term plans, supply feedback to customers

15        who want to connect to the SPS system, and coordinate with Southwest Power Pool,

16        Inc. (“Southwest Power Pool”) on regional policy and cost allocation issues

17        affecting SPS. My responsibilities as far as Southwest Power Pool is concerned

18        include representing SPS through membership participation in several Southwest

                                             of
                                      Jarred J. Cooley

 1        Power Pool member committees and helping direct overall strategic positions in the

 2        various stakeholder working groups.

 3   Q.   Please describe your educational background.

 4   A.   I received my Bachelor of Science degree in Electrical Engineering in 2010 from

 5        the University of Minnesota – Twin Cities.

 6   Q.   Please describe your professional experience.

 7   A.   In 2010, I started full-time as an engineer in the Transmission Planning department

 8        with Xcel Energy, based in Minneapolis, Minnesota. In 2018, I relocated to

 9        Amarillo, Texas and became Manager, Transmission Planning South, leading the

10        transmission planning department that was focused on the SPS service territory. In

11        October 2021, I took on my current role of Director, Strategic Planning for SPS.

12   Q.   Do you hold a professional license?

13   A.   Yes. I am a registered Professional Engineer in the State of Minnesota.

14   Q.   Have you filed testimony before any regulatory authorities?

15   A.   Yes. I submitted pre-filed written testimony to the New Mexico Public Regulation

16        Commission (“Commission”) on SPS’s behalf in Case Nos. 25-00066-UT, 22-

17        00286-UT, 20-00238-UT, 20-00085-UT, 19--00170-UT, and 19-00157-UT. I

18        testified in the hearing on the settlement in Case No. 19-00170-UT. Additionally, I

 3   Q.   What is your assignment in this proceeding?

 4   A.   I describe and support SPS’s request to recover (1) the Schedule 1-A expenses

 5        charged by Southwest Power Pool for the services provided to SPS by Southwest

 6        Power Pool and (2) Schedule 11 transmission expenses and revenues. I also

 7        describe the recent increase in Southwest Power Pool’s minimum planning reserve

10   A.   I recommend the Commission allow SPS to recover $8,219,771 on a New Mexico

11        retail basis ($16,539,293 total company) of Southwest Power Pool Schedule 1-A

12        expenses for the Future Test Year. 1 SPS calculated that amount by applying the

13        2025 year-over-year average Schedule 1-A rate increase of 5.74% annually into the

14        Future Test Year, using forecasted billing determinants. 2 I also discuss the

15        Southwest Power Pool transmission planning processes and recommend the

 6   Q.   How were New Mexico retail jurisdictional amounts in your testimony and

 7        attachments calculated?

 8   A.   Throughout this testimony, I quantify the Schedule 1-A expense and asset amounts

12        responsible for calculating jurisdictional allocation percentages that apply to the

13        various cost components in the cost of service. My staff and I conferred with Ms.

14        Johnson and her staff to determine the New Mexico retail jurisdictional amounts

15        presented in my testimony and attachments. If the percentages used to allocate

16        amounts to the New Mexico retail jurisdiction change, those new allocation

17        percentages will need to be applied to the total company numbers to derive updated

18        New Mexico retail amounts. Attachment JJC-1 contains the total company numbers

 1                 III.   SOUTHWEST POWER POOL SERVICES

 2   Q.   Please describe Southwest Power Pool and the services it provides to its

 3        members.

 4   A.   Southwest Power Pool, which is a FERC-approved Regional Transmission

 5        Organization (“RTO”), is an Arkansas non-profit corporation with its principal

 6        place of business in Little Rock, Arkansas. Southwest Power Pool has more than

 7        120 members, which include electric cooperatives, federal agencies, independent

 8        power producers, independent electric transmission companies, investor-owned

 9        electric utilities, marketers, municipal utilities, state authorities, large retail

10        customers, and contract participants.

11               As an RTO, Southwest Power Pool provides several services to its

12        members, including:

13                   •    Reliability coordination;
14                   •    Tariff administration;
15                   •    Regional scheduling;
16                   •    Transmission expansion planning;
17                   •    Market operation;
18                   •    Contingency reserve sharing;
19                   •    Generation interconnection studies;


                                                   7
                                    Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                     Direct Testimony
                                             of
                                      Jarred J. Cooley

 1                   •   Scheduling authority function;
 2                   •   Compliance;
 3                   •   Training; and
 4                   •   Outage coordination.

 5   Q.   How are Southwest Power Pool’s policies, rules, and tariffs developed?

 6   A.   Southwest Power Pool is a member-driven organization. As a result, various

 7        committees exist within Southwest Power Pool to develop policy, rules, and tariff

 8        provisions related to a wide variety of topics. The primary role of Southwest Power

 9        Pool stakeholder committees and working groups is to drive major initiatives that

10        improve or enhance Southwest Power Pool operations. The stakeholder process

11        also focuses on planning for the future. The various committees and working groups

12        provide recommendations to the Southwest Power Pool independent Board of

13        Directors on technical issues. The committees are further composed of working

14        groups, steering committees, task forces, advisory groups, and user forums. The

15        committees and groups are made up of representatives derived from the diverse

16        subset of Southwest Power Pool members, including SPS. An organizational chart

17        of Southwest Power Pool committees and working groups is attached to my

18        testimony as Attachment JJC-2. Additional groups and details can be found on the

19        www.SPP.org webpage.

                                                8
                                    Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                     Direct Testimony
                                             of
                                      Jarred J. Cooley

 1   Q.   Do state retail rate regulators have a role in the Southwest Power Pool

 2        member-driven process?

 3   A.   Yes. The Regional State Committee (“RSC”) is composed of retail regulators

 4        across the Southwest Power Pool footprint. The RSC has its own working group,

 5        the Cost Allocation Working Group, which is made up of staff members of the retail

 6        regulatory authorities. The RSC actively engages in a broad range of issues where

 7        Southwest Power Pool has ceded authority, including transmission planning and

 8        cost allocation, resource adequacy, allocation of transmission rights, and market

 9        evolution issues. For example, the RSC: (1) establishes the approach for resource

10        adequacy across the entire region and with respect to transmission planning; (2)

11        decides whether transmission upgrades for remote resources will be included in the

12        regional transmission planning process; and (3) determines the role of transmission

13        owners in proposing transmission upgrades in the regional planning process.

14   Q.   Have the services that SPS receives from Southwest Power Pool changed since

15        SPS’s last rate case, Case No. 22-00286-UT?

16   A.   No. As a member of Southwest Power Pool, SPS continues to receive the same

17        services that the Commission reviewed in SPS’s last case.




                                               9

                                     Direct Testimony
                                             of
                                      Jarred J. Cooley

 1   Q.   Do SPS’s customers obtain benefits by SPS being a member of the Southwest

 2        Power Pool?

 3   A.   Yes. SPS’s customers benefit by having access to a larger pool of generation

 4        resources as part of the Southwest Power Pool’s Integrated Marketplace, allowing

 5        low-cost generation to serve SPS’s load. Additionally, SPS is able to decrease the

 6        amount of generation reserves needed in the event of a sudden resource outage

 7        because it is part of a reserve sharing arrangement. Finally, Southwest Power Pool

 8        is responsible for overseeing transmission planning studies, the generator

 9        interconnection queue, transmission service requests, load interconnection

10        requests, and outage coordination.

11   Q.   Does SPS make payments to the Southwest Power Pool as part of its

12        membership?

13   A.   Yes. SPS pays Southwest Power Pool an administrative fee through Schedule 1-A

14        of the Southwest Power Pool Open Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”) and is

15        allocated transmission costs and revenues associated with transmission

16        infrastructure within the Southwest Power Pool under Schedule 11.




                                               10

 1        A.     Schedule 1-A Administrative Fee
 2   Q.   What is the Southwest Power Pool administrative fee?

 3   A.   The Southwest Power Pool applies an administrative fee to all transmission service

 4        customers to cover the expenses that Southwest Power Pool incurs for the services

 5        it provides under its OATT, such as transmission service, tariff administration, and

 6        facilitation of Southwest Power Pool’s Integrated Marketplace. The fee is set

 7        annually by the Southwest Power Pool Board of Directors based on the next year’s

 8        expected budget, including reconciliation from the previous year’s over-or-under-

 9        collection.

10   Q.   How does Southwest Power Pool collect these administrative fees?

11   A.   Southwest Power Pool collects these fees through Schedule 1-A of its OATT.

12   Q.   How are Schedule 1-A charges assessed?

13   A.   Starting January 1, 2021, Southwest Power Pool separated the Schedule 1-A

14        charges into four separate charges. They are:

15           •   Schedule 1-A1 - Transmission Administration Service;

16           •   Schedule 1-A2 - Transmission Congestion Rights Administration Service;

17           •   Schedule 1-A3 - Integrated Marketplace Clearing Administration Service;
18               and



                                              11

                                     Direct Testimony
                                             of
                                      Jarred J. Cooley

1            •   Schedule 1-A4 - Integrated Marketplace Facilitation Administration
2                Service.

3         Schedule 1-A1 charges are divided between FERC Accounts 561.4 and 561.8.

4         Schedules 1-A2, 1-A3, and 1-A4 are charged to FERC Account 575.7.

5    Q.   Please describe the different charges within Schedule 1-A.

6    A.   Schedule 1-A1, Transmission Administration Service, is intended to recover the

7         Southwest Power Pool’s administration costs related to the provision of

8         Transmission Service. Schedule 1-A2, Transmission Congestion Rights

 9        Administration Service, is intended to recover the Southwest Power Pool’s

10        administration costs related to congestion rights in the Integrated Marketplace.

11        Holders of Transmission Congestion Rights (“TCRs”) are charged the portion of

12        Southwest Power Pool’s administration costs for items such as TCR auction, TCR

13        simultaneous feasibility tests, and the administration of a secondary market for

14        TCRs. Schedule 1-A3, Integrated Marketplace Clearing Administration Service, is

15        intended to recover the Southwest Power Pool’s administration costs associated

16        with providing market settlements, credit evaluation, market monitoring, and

17        customer service to Integrated Marketplace participants. Schedule 1-A, Integrated

18        Marketplace Facilitation Administration Service, is intended to recover the

19        Southwest Power Pool’s administration costs associated with facilitating the day-

                                             12

                                     Direct Testimony
                                             of
                                      Jarred J. Cooley

 1        ahead and real-time energy and ancillary services markets, and the reliability unit

 2        commitment processes for Integrated Marketplace participants. Ms. Johnson

 3        discusses how SPS proposes to recover each of these administrative fees in her

 4        direct testimony.

 5   Q.   What was the Base Period amount of Schedule 1-A expense?

 6   A.   The Base Period amount of Schedule 1-A expense was $6,848,405 on a New

 7        Mexico retail basis ($15,200,030 total company). I calculated that amount by

 8        multiplying the per megawatt-hour (“MWh”) fee charged in calendar year 2024 to

 9        the MWh of load consumed by SPS customers during the last six months of 2024,

10        and by multiplying the per MWh fee charged in calendar year 2025 to the MWh of

11        load consumed by SPS customers during the first six months of 2025. I then added

12        the two amounts together to get the Base Period Schedule 1-A expenses.

14        Schedule 1-A expense?

15   A.   Yes. SPS decreased the Base Period amount by $27,294 on a New Mexico Retail

16        basis ($59,328 total company) to address administrative credits for production

17        months outside of the Base Period. This adjustment normalized the Base Period

1    Q.   Are the Schedule 1-A amounts charged by the Southwest Power Pool

 2        reasonable and necessary costs of providing service?

 3   A.   Yes. The Schedule 1-A administrative fee, which covers the transmission planning

4         cost, tariff administrator responsibilities, and operation of the Southwest Power

5         Pool Integrated Market, benefits SPS customers by allowing SPS to gain greater

6         access to economic market resources and by enhancing the reliability of the grid.

 7        B.     Schedule 11 Allocation of Southwest                        Power      Pool
 8               Transmission Costs and Revenues
 9   Q.   Please discuss the Southwest Power Pool’s Transmission Expansion Planning

10        function.

11   A.   As a FERC-designated RTO, the Southwest Power Pool has the responsibility to

12        create regional transmission expansion plans. With its members, regulators, and

13        stakeholders, the Southwest Power Pool creates planning models and studies that

14        determine what and when new transmission is needed to meet the region’s long-

15        and near-term needs. This planning activity creates a cost-effective, flexible, and

16        robust transmission network.




                                              16
                                    Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                     Direct Testimony
                                             of
                                      Jarred J. Cooley

 1   Q.   Please summarize the process the Southwest Power Pool uses for Transmission

 2        Expansion Planning.

 3   A.   As outlined in Attachment O of the Southwest Power Pool OATT, the Southwest

 4        Power Pool performs a variety of different planning processes to identify new

 5        transmission facilities. The planning processes include: (1) Transmission Service

 6        Requests; (2) Generator Interconnection Requests; (3) requests pursuant to

 7        Attachment AQ and Attachment AX of the OATT; (4) the Integrated Transmission

 8        Planning (“ITP”) Assessment; (5) the Balanced Portfolio process; (6) the high

 9        priority study process; (7) requests for Sponsored Upgrades; (8) the 20-Year

10        Assessment; (9) the evaluation of proposed Interregional Projects; and (10) the

11        Generator Retirement Process. The ITP Assessment typically produces the largest

12        amount of new transmission facilities to member utilities. Attachment J of the

13        Southwest Power Pool OATT outlines how cost are recovered for new facilities.

14   Q.   What is the Integrated Transmission Planning (“ITP”) Assessment?

15   A.   The ITP Assessment is an annual study used to identify transmission solutions that

16        meet near- and long-term reliability, economic, public policy, and operational

17        transmission needs. The study utilizes models built to represent reliability and

18        economic model forecasts two years, five years, and ten years into the future. The


                                              17
                                         Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                          Direct Testimony
                                                  of
                                           Jarred J. Cooley

 1        purpose of the ITP Assessment is to develop a Southwest Power Pool region-wide

 2        transmission plan that addresses the reliability and economic needs looking out 10

 3        years in a cost-effective manner. The objectives of the ITP Assessment are: 4

 4            •   Resolve reliability criteria violations;
 5            •   Improve access to markets;
 6            •   Improve interconnections with Southwest Power Pool neighbors;
 7            •   Meet expected load-growth demands;
 8            •   Facilitate or respond to expected facility retirements;
 9            •   Synergize with the Generator Interconnection (GI), Aggregate
10                Transmission Service Studies (ATSS), and Delivery Point Assessment
11                (DPA) processes;

12            •   Address persistent operational issues;
13            •   Facilitate continuity in the overall transmission expansion plan; and
14            •   Facilitate a cost effective, responsive, and flexible transmission network.

15   Q.   What is a high-priority study?

16   A.   A high-priority study is done at the request of stakeholders or the Southwest Power

17        Pool staff in response to critical current or future transmission issues. Network

18        upgrades identified through a high-priority study, as directed for construction by

 3        The last high priority study, the High Priority Incremental Load Study (“HPILS”)

 4        that was focused on significant load growth primarily driven by oil and gas

 5        development, was completed in 2014.

 6   Q.   What is a Sponsored Upgrade?

 7   A.   Sponsored Upgrades are network upgrades requested by a Transmission Customer

 8        or other entity that are not previously or currently included in other Southwest

 9        Power Pool planning processes. Any entity may request that a Sponsored Upgrade

10        be built. The Southwest Power Pool evaluates the impact of any Sponsored Upgrade

11        on transmission system reliability and identifies any necessary mitigation of these

12        impacts. The project sponsor must be willing to assume the cost of the Sponsored

13        Upgrade, study costs, and any cost associated with necessary mitigation.

14   Q.   How active has SPS been in Southwest Power Pool’s planning process?

15   A.   SPS personnel are active in every stage of the Southwest Power Pool planning

16        processes, from study scope development to model build efforts, to providing

17        project solutions and alternatives, cost estimates, finalizing portfolios and reports,

18        and accepting Notification to Construct (“NTC”). The SPS personnel work with the

 1        Southwest Power Pool planning department in developing projects that meet the

 2        needs of the SPS area.

 3   Q.   How are entities selected to construct transmission facilities?

 4   A.   As part of FERC Order No. 1000, all public utility transmission providers

 5        (including RTOs) were required to remove from their FERC-jurisdictional tariffs

 6        and agreements any provisions that granted a “federal right of first refusal” to a

 7        current (“incumbent”) public utility transmission provider to construct regional

 8        transmission facilities if the costs of such facilities are allocated to customers

 9        outside of the incumbent utility’s retail distribution service territory or footprint.

10        The removal of the federal right of first refusal potentially allows non-incumbent

11        transmission developers to compete for the right to construct certain transmission

12        lines. Attachment Y of the Southwest Power Pool OATT outlines the process in

13        which projects are awarded to different Transmission Owners. Broadly, if the new

14        transmission facility is less than 100 kilovolt (“kV”), is a rebuild, is an expansion

15        of an existing facility, is needed for reliability reasons within three years (“Short-

16        Term Reliability Project”), or if the state in which the project is being built has a

17        state-level “right of first refusal,” the project is likely be assigned to the incumbent

18        Transmission Owner. If the project does not meet those criteria, the Southwest

                                              of
                                       Jarred J. Cooley

 1        Power Pool’s Transmission Owner Selection Process may be triggered.

2         Transmission projects from studies like Generation Interconnection Requests and

3         Sponsored Upgrades are excluded from the Transmission Owner Selection Process

4         because the costs for the network upgrades are assigned to a single customer, not

5         regionally allocated.

 6   Q.   Please describe Transmission Owner Selection Process as administrated by the

 7        Southwest Power Pool.

 8   A.   As a part of the Southwest Power Pool compliance filings in FERC Docket Nos.

 1        IV.   CHANGE IN MINIMUM PLANNING RESERVE MARGIN

 2   Q.   What do you discuss in this section of your testimony?

 3   A.   I discuss recent changes in Southwest Power Pool’s minimum planning reserve

 4        margin requirements and explain how those changes affect SPS’s capacity position.

 5        SPS Witness Justin L. Gable also discusses Southwest Power Pool’s increased

 6        minimum planning reserve margin requirement and particularly SPS’s proposal to

 7        extend the service lives of existing resources and to add new solar and BESS

 8        resources approved in Case No. 23-00252-UT; new solar, BESS, and thermal units

 9        pursuant to pending Case No. 25-00066-UT; and other resources SPS has identified

10        in its 2024 request for proposals or expects to identify through a request for

11        proposals issued in 2025. The purpose of my testimony is to discuss Southwest

12        Power Pool’s minimum planning reserve margin in more detail.

13   Q.   What is the basis for establishing Southwest Power Pool’s minimum planning

14        reserve margin requirement?

15   A.   Southwest Power Pool outlines its resource adequacy process through Attachment

16        AA of the Southwest Power Pool OATT. Southwest Power Pool performs a loss-

17        of-load-expectation study for the Southwest Power Pool area and determines what


                                             28
                                     Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                      Direct Testimony
                                              of
                                       Jarred J. Cooley

 1        level of reserves would be required to meet the industry standard of loss of load one

 2        day every ten years due to generation capacity and deliverability. Southwest Power

 3        Pool is transitioning to performing studies on the reserve margin requirements

 4        annually to determine whether the value is still adequate and to hopefully provide

 5        a better glidepath to potential future step changes.

 6   Q.   What is the history of the Southwest Power Pool recommended planning

 7        reserves?

 8   A.   In July 2022, the Regional State Committee and the Southwest Power Pool Board

 9        of Directors approved a proposal to increase the planning reserve margin

10        requirement from 12% to 15% effective for the summer of 2023. In 2024, the

11        Regional State Committee and Board of Directors again approved an increase that

12        will take effect in summer 2026. Under the new planning reserve margin

13        requirements, load responsible entities will have to maintain a summer planning

14        reserve margin of at least 16%, and a winter planning reserve margin of at least

15        36%. This is a notable change because it is the first time Southwest Power Pool has

16        set a separate winter planning reserve margin.

 1   Q.   Do Southwest Power Pool criteria specifically require a 16% summer and 36%

 2        winter planning reserve margin?

 3   A.   The 16% and 36% planning reserve margins are the minimum value necessary for

 4        each load responsible entity in order to reach the region-wide requirement. If a load

 5        responsible entity, such as SPS, does not have enough capacity to meet the planning

 6        reserve margin, that entity is required to pay a deficiency payment. Furthermore, in

 7        some situations, carrying only the minimum required reserves would be detrimental

 8        to the load (i.e., customers) in specific areas.

 9   Q.   What amount of increased reserves reflects the 16% summer minimum

10        planning reserve requirement and how does that impact the SPS system?

11   A.   As discussed by SPS witness Mr. Gable, if a 16% minimum reserve margin

12        requirement is applied to the planning forecast, SPS will need an additional 46 MW

13        in 2026 to meet the capacity need. Mr. Gable discusses how SPS is satisfying this

14        requirement.

 1   Q.   What amount of increased reserves reflects the 36% winter minimum

 2        planning reserve requirement and how does that impact the SPS system?

 3   A.   To meet the new 36% winter planning reserve margin requirement in winter 2026-

 4        2027, SPS will need an additional 887 MW of accredited generation compared to

 5        what was required under the 15% PRM requirement.

6    Q.   Should the Southwest Power Pool minimum planning reserve margin

7         requirement be used to determine whether SPS’s system has capacity that

 8        exceeds the generation needed to appropriately and cost-effectively serve its

 9        customers?

10   A.   No. The Southwest Power Pool planning reserve margin requirement is a minimum

11        requirement, not a maximum or a target, and it does not fully capture all the

12        resource needs in the SPS footprint. Additionally, while SPS must exceed that

13        minimum threshold, that threshold does not dictate all of SPS’s planning. SPS

14        conducts resource planning to prudently provide energy to customers—not just to

15        have capacity—and to meet applicable Renewable Portfolio Standards

16        requirements. Finally, given the features of SPS’s service territory and system, such

17        as system topology, import capabilities, load and generation siting, and congestion

                                     Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                      Direct Testimony
                                              of
                                       Jarred J. Cooley

 1        management needs, just meeting the Southwest Power Pool minimum requirement

 2        would not necessarily ensure reliable service for customers.

 3   Q.   Is the location of the SPS system, and the location of SPS’s generating

 4        resources within the system, important in evaluating SPS’s generating

 5        capacity?

 6   A.   Yes. Because of SPS’s location within Southwest Power Pool and the existing

 7        transmission constraints, it is important to consider the need for generation in

 8        particular areas and not just the total capacity of SPS’s generating fleet. SPS is on

 9        the furthest, most remote southwestern edge of the Eastern Interconnection and is

10        the southernmost utility system in the Southwest Power Pool’s 14-state footprint.

11        The design of the transmission system depends on the placement of SPS’s

12        generation resources, SPS’s load, and the transmission tie-lines back to the rest of

13        Southwest Power Pool. For example, generation located in New Mexico or the

14        southern part of SPS’s system helps reduce the flow of energy into that

15        southernmost area of the system. Having generation in close proximity to load can

16        help balance resource planning needs with the necessary transmission construction

17        that may be required to maintain system reliability. Although the transmission

18        capability between the SPS service area and the rest of the Southwest Power Pool

19        footprint has been greatly improved, SPS is still affected more than other utilities

 1        when one or more of the 345 kV tie lines into the SPS system is out of service for

 2        maintenance or any other reason. Considering the location of the SPS system

 3        relative to the rest of the Southwest Power Pool geography, the SPS transmission

 4        system topology, and the location of load and of the SPS generation facilities within

 5        the SPS footprint; SPS likely would have required significantly more transmission

 6        expansion if there was less generation available within the SPS footprint to serve

 7        the load.

 8   Q.   Does SPS continue to see increased load growth on its system?

 9   A.   Yes. As discussed by SPS Witnesses Casey S. Meeks and John M. Goodenough,

10        oil and gas development in the New Mexico portion of the Permian Basin is still

11        growing and in the future SPS will need additional generation capacity on its system

12        to serve that continued load growth. As noted previously, siting future generation

13        near this load will likely be beneficial to SPS’s system operations.
